candidates.raw_excerpt: With both solid rocket boosters fully stacked and all four RS-25 engines now installed on the Core Stage, NASA is preparing to mate the stage to the boosters and form the short stack that will roll to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test. The test, expected in the coming months, will also give the Artemis III crew their first full launch-day rehearsal on the pad ahead of the targeted no-earlier-than June 2027 mission. Engineers with NASA’s Exploration Ground Systems finished stacking the twin five-segment boosters on September 30 by mating the aerodynamic nose cones to the left and right forward assemblies inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at Kennedy Space Center. Each forward assembly includes the nose cone, a forward skirt housing avionics, and a frustum containing the separation motors. The boosters, built by Northrop Grumman, will deliver more than 75 percent of total SLS thrust at liftoff from Pad 39B. Stacking on Mobile Launcher 1 began in mid-July with the aft segments. Teams added the aft-center, center, and forward-center segments through August before completing the stacks with the forward assemblies. The boosters now stand complete in High Bay 3. Core Stage processing has kept pace in High Bay 2. After the tank section arrived from Michoud Assembly Facility and was mated to the engine section, teams completed installation of the four RS-25 engines. The next step is fitting the systems tunnel that runs the length of the stage and carries the pyrotechnic cabling for the single-use quick-disconnects used at liftoff. Once that work is finished, the Core Stage will be mated to the boosters in the coming weeks to create the short stack. This configuration leaves off the upper-stage adapters, spacer, and Orion spacecraft. NASA plans to roll the short stack to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test, during which the launch team will practice propellant loading timelines and procedures. candidates.raw_excerpt: Most planetary scientists will tell you the heyday of Venus exploration was more than a generation ago. That is about to change. Two NASA missions are on track to launch to Venus in the early 2030s. The first, known as the Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging (DAVINCI), is now scheduled for launch in December 2030, a year earlier than previously planned. A second mission, Venus Emissivity, Radio science, InSAR, Topography, And Spectroscopy (VERITAS), will follow with a launch in November 2032 to map the Venusian surface by radar from orbit. The European Space Agency is building another orbiter, Envision, for launch to Venus in 2032. The Venus armada might get started as soon as next year, when Rocket Lab aims to launch a privately funded probe to search for signs of organic material in the planet's clouds. candidates.title: Scientists discover that some of the universe's biggest explosions may have never happened at all
candidates.raw_excerpt: Now you see them, now you don't. Scientists have discovered that some of the universe's most powerful explosions, hypernovas, may not happen at all. These explosions, known as hypernovas , were first proposed to explain unusual stars in the halo of our galaxy, the Milky Way , and in a neighboring dwarf galaxy. It was suggested that these stars could only form from the debris of an explosion 10 times more powerful than the 'average' supernovas . The team behind these new findings suggests that ordinary supernovas could actually account for these stars when the uneven or non-spherical way they fling out matter is considered. "If we look at a supernova today, the star's materials are not spread evenly. Oxygen might predominantly fly in one direction, sulphur in another. New stars might form from a mix of pieces of the supernova, not its overall mix of elements," team leader Anmol Aggarwal of University College London (UCL) said in a statement. "We developed mathematical models that took account of this and found in all cases that stars with a very unusual mix of ingredients were most likely formed from ordinary supernovas. "All the evidence we see for hypernovae is suddenly gone." Hypernova vs. supernova: What's the difference? Supernovas occur when massive stars run out of fuel for nuclear fusion , effectively ending their lives. This results in the star's core collapsing, sending shockwaves rippling through its outer layers, causing explosions we call supernovas. Hypernovas are proposed to occur in a similar way, but for an even more massive and rapidly spinning star. This results in a vastly more energetic explosion. When supernovas or hypernovas happen, they fling elements that the dying star has forged throughout its lifetime into their surrounding cosmic environments. These elements eventually become the building blocks of the next generation of stars. That means analyzing the chemical signatures of stars can tell stellar scientists about their family histories.

candidates.title: OpenAI engineer arrested over alleged hidden recording device
candidates.raw_excerpt:
An OpenAI engineer has been arrested after allegedly installing a hidden audio recording device inside the company's office in San Francisco, the United States, according to statements released by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) and OpenAI.

OpenAI said in a post on X that it had "discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices" and "referred the matter to the FBI."

There is currently no evidence that the individual improperly accessed or exfiltrated model weights, source code or customer data, the company added.

OpenAI's security team discovered the device on September 30 during a routine inspection. The employee, a Saudi national, was arrested on October 9, the DOJ said.

According to the DOJ, Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer who had worked for OpenAI since July 2025, allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television in an executive conference room.

Closed-circuit television footage from the company's office showed that Alfozan "appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device's discovery," although he was not authorized to attend meetings held there.

He also used a "productivity tool" to search for information about OpenAI's office buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, schedules and people's locations, according to the DOJ statement.

Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan had reportedly worked at other major technology companies, including Meta and Microsoft.

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

The plan sets out four major initiatives covering improvements to the protection and management system, more targeted conservation, technology-driven innovation, and the preservation and creative use of ancient-tree culture.

By 2030, Beijing aims to establish a standardized database of ancient and notable trees and create 10 ecological and cultural landmarks centered on ancient trees in the old city, besides building 100 ancient-tree habitat gardens and villages. The city also plans to carry out preventive protection and restoration work on more than 3,000 trees and collect and preserve genetic resources from 100 rare and endangered ancient trees.

To reduce the risk of trees falling during extreme weather, the plan calls for improved emergency protection mechanisms. Inspections will focus on trees in busy areas, including roadsides, parks and scenic spots, as well as trees at high risk of falling due to internal trunk decay, leaning trunks or an imbalance between roots and crowns. candidates.raw_excerpt: It’s not just your electricity bill that could be going up — it sounds like the massive boom in AI data centers is making practically everything more expensive. As the Washington Post reports , officials at the Federal Reserve are starting to sing a different tune after blaming president Donald Trump’s tariff war on rising prices, admitting that the explosion in “AI-related investments” is contributing to inflationary pressures. That’s on top of Trump’s Iran war already sending the price of oil soaring. Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee told Semafor that AI-tied inflation is “jumping out of its lane.” “Prices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,” he said. “I’m getting increasingly nervous that that’s just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.” In economics, overheating occurs when aggregate demand outpaces productive capacity, leading to demand-side inflation, higher prices, and eventually reduced demand and consumption. In the worst case scenario, overheating can even trigger a recession . “It takes a long time for overheated demand to get going, and once it’s going, it’s hard to get rid of that,” Goolsbee added. While the prices for groceries have yet to be directly impacted, economists are wondering whether it’s only a matter of time. Worse yet, whether raising the interest rate, which makes borrowing more expensive and lowers consumer spending, will be able to meaningfully address rising inflation, is also starting to look less like a certain bet. The Fed raised interest rates in September, the first time in three years, as inflation proves tough to beat. Futures markets expect yet another increase later this month, according to Reuters . Meanwhile, the tens of billions of dollars being spent on AI data centers are starting to mask some fundamental problems plaguing the US economy, triggering fears over what it could look like if the AI bubble were to burst. candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the " Whirlpool Galaxy , " also known as Messier 51, or M51. Charles Messier was scanning the sky for objects that could confuse comet hunters when he catalogued the galaxy as M51. However, Messier wasn't able to see the spiral structure, and he didn't identify it as a galaxy. Seventy-two years later, another astronomer named William Parsons saw the whirlpool shape, but he thought it was a spiral nebula. Eventually, Edwin Hubble found out that M51 and other features like it were actually galaxies. Spiral galaxy M51 (NGC 5194), The Whirlpool Galaxy, displays its long arms which consist of stars and gas laced with dust arranged in long lanes, in this view from the Hubble Space Telescope. The smaller galaxy to the right is NGC 5195, which is actually more distant than M51, and not next door. (Image credit: NASA/ESA/S. Beckwith/Hubble Heritage Team/STScI/AURA) Why it mattered The Whirlpool Galaxy is located about 31 million light-years from Earth and just might be the textbook case of a spiral galaxy . But in 1773, it was just one of 51 (at the time of its discovery) of "comet-like 'objects to avoid'" in the night sky. The Whirlpool Galaxy's designation as M51 marks it as the 51st non-comet object catalogued by Messier, who was the chief astronomer of the Marine Observatory in Paris dedicated to studying comets. According to a NASA account , Messier stumbled across his first non-comet object, M1 (also known as the Crab Nebula ), while studying a comet in 1758. The objects looked like fuzzy blobs like comets, but didn't move like a comet. candidates.title: Earth's poles shifted surprisingly fast during the age of dinosaurs, ancient sea levels reveal
candidates.raw_excerpt: The location of Earth's geographic poles has changed several times over the past 320 million years in a process known as true polar wander, according to measurements of ancient flooding brought about by sea level changes resulting from our planet's crust shifting relative to Earth's spin axis. Such a shift can affect climate, both on local scales and globally, as regions that were by the poles find themselves moving down to lower latitudes and vice versa. This can then affect atmospheric circulation patterns, which affect climate across the world. The changes would have affected the environments in which life developed and evolved, from the age of the dinosaurs through to some of our oldest primate ancestors. True polar wander is not the same as a change in the rotational axis of the Earth . Currently, Earth spins at an angle of 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit around the sun, and this rotational axis can vary periodically over tens of thousands of years as a result of the Milankovitch cycles caused by the gravitational pull of the sun and planets. True polar wander is different. Here, the angle of Earth's spin axis does not change relative to its orbital plane. Instead, Earth's crust and mantle shift relative to that rotational axis. This is because Earth is not perfectly spherical. Instead, it is oblate, with Earth's rotation causing the equator to bulge out and the poles to slightly flatten. Because Earth is not spherical, it has multiple axes of inertia, the largest one being aligned with the rotational axis. These axes need to be balanced to prevent Earth's rotation from becoming chaotic. However, plate tectonics and indeed the Milankovitch cycles can upset that balance of mass, for example by causing more continental crust to congregate in one hemisphere than another. candidates.title: China releases report on ethical governance for embodied AI
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China on Tuesday released a report on the ethics of embodied intelligence – the field that covers machines that can sense, decide and act in the physical world.

The report treats embodied intelligence ethics as part of broader AI ethics. It flags six risk areas: harm to human autonomy, to social relationships and to development rights; physical injury and threats to public safety; privacy violations and misuse of personal information; bias, discrimination and exclusion from services; identity misidentification and overestimation of capabilities; and unclear accountability, with incidents hard to reconstruct.

The report defines five risk levels, R1 through R5, based on how serious the consequences are. It also sets out six basic governance principles: human-centered, safe and controllable, privacy-protecting, fair and inclusive, transparent and explainable, and accountable and traceable.

Ethical requirements should be built into every stage of an embodied AI product's lifecycle – design, R&D, deployment, operation and service, and decommissioning – and each stage should have clear protection requirements and assigned responsibilities, said Zhang Shizong, deputy director of the IT Research Center at the China Electronics Standardization Institute (CESI).

Zhang said the safeguards work in three ways. Limits on what the machine can do to protect physical safety. Controls on what it can collect to protect sensory data. Clear signals that it's a machine, plus ways to switch it off, preserve the user's ability to choose.

China will accelerate work on national standards including guidelines for ethical governance for AI and embodied intelligence, Zhang said.

What is it? Menon's photo reveals spectacular pink, purple and red auroras glowing in Earth's upper atmosphere above a sparse dappling of city lights, subtly blurred by the motion of the orbital spacecraft over the course of the exposure. Bright stars glimmer between the solar panels and outer hulls of the ISS and visiting spacecraft, painted purple by the auroral display. It's definitely more immersive." Why is it amazing? Menon captured the auroras during a period of heightened geomagnetic activity, after several coronal mass ejections (CMEs) struck Earth's magnetic field, triggering geomagnetic storms ranging from minor (G1) to strong (G3) over the weekend. During geomagnetic storms, more charged particles are accelerated along Earth's magnetic field lines toward the polar regions, where they collide with gases in the upper atmosphere; they excite them, causing them to release energy as light and producing spectacular auroral displays. The blue-purple colors seen in Menon's image are largely produced by nitrogen at altitudes of around 60-120 miles (100-200 kilometers) , while the red hue comes from oxygen atoms higher up, typically above 125 miles (200 kilometers). candidates.raw_excerpt: Hydrogen may be the most common element in the cosmos, but scientists could use it to do something unique: uncover the nature of dark energy, the mysterious force driving the accelerating expansion of the universe. This new line of dark energy investigation comes from the fact that researchers have determined that the CHIME (Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) project can detect the faint radio glow of hydrogen from the universe's distant past. Not only does this represent a faster and much less expensive way to investigate dark energy, but it is a major milestone for CHIME. The instrument was specifically devised to investigate dark energy and its pervasive influence. "This is a completely new technique for probing the cosmos, delivered by an instrument that was conceived and built by Canadians," CHIME principal investigator Mark Halpern of the University of British Columbia said in a statement . "It's a bold new step in the global cosmology program and a Canadian success story." Why is dark energy so problematic? Dark energy is the mysterious force that is accelerating the expansion of the universe . It is so problematic for scientists because it started acting on the fabric of space only after the expansion triggered by the Big Bang had halted. That's akin to pushing a child on a swing, watching it stop, and then seeing the swing start up again without a push. And, not only that, but the swing starts oscillating faster and faster. Consider scientists akin to very worried parents, who would really like to know where this ghostly push came from and how it is going to proceed. Just as, if the push on the swing continues, the child could end up in the bushes, or in orbit, the strengthening of dark energy could result in the cold death of the cosmos, or even a " Big Rip " scenario that sees space shredded. SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket to launch 27 Starlink satellites into orbit from California
candidates.raw_excerpt: A Falcon 9 rocket stands ready for launch from Vandenberg in this file photo. Image: SpaceX. SpaceX will launch a Falcon 9 rocket Monday from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, carrying another batch of Starlink satellites. Liftoff off of the Starlink 15-25 mission from Space Launch Complex 4 East is scheduled for 5:28 p.m. PDT (8:28 p.m. EDT / 0028 UTC). The rocket will head on a southerly trajectory along the California coast as it targets an orbit inclined 70 degrees to the Equator. Spaceflight Now will have live coverage starting about 30 minutes prior to launch. The first-stage booster, serial number B1088, launching for a 20th time, will land on the drone ship ‘Of Course I Still Love You’ nearly 8.5 minutes into the flight. The booster previously flew the NROL-126, Transporter-12, SPHEREx, NROL-57 and USSF-366 mission, plus 14 previous Starlink delivery runs. If all goes according to plan the 27 Starlink V2 Mini Optimized satellites will be deployed into a 266 kilometer high orbit a little more than an hour after liftoff.
